newsitem.title: GERMANY: INTERVIEW - Chrysler seeks European expansion.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Chrysler seeks European expansion.

text.p: Chrysler Corp, citing strong demand for its popular minivans and Jeep vehicles, said on Tuesday it was strengthening its European dealer network in hopes of doubling sales within the next five to seven years.

Chrysler Europe President Timothy Adams also told Reuters in a telephone interview from the U.S. carmaker's Brussels European headquarters that Chrysler has no plans to buy or set up new vehicle production sites in Europe.
The carmaker has been rumoured as a potential buyer of idled vehicle production sites in Europe.

"Although there will be variations, we expect our business to grow significantly over the next five to seven years," Adams said. "We think our business could double over that time."

Chrysler has a production site in Graz, Austria where Chrysler minivans and Jeep Grand Cherokees are built. Adams said capacity at the facility, which is 100,000 vehicles per year, was not fully utilised at the moment.

About 60 percent of the vehicles built in Graz are sold in Europe, while the balance are exported outside of Europe. Adams said Chrysler's strategy would continue to be to import other models from the United States.
"We have made the decision to keep our fixed costs as low as possible. It is still the strategy to source a lot of our products from the United States," Adams said.

"Competition here is tough and we are not intending to buy market share. We want to build the business profitably and this plan provides us more flexiblity than if we were trying to sell capacity," he said.

Chrysler still pales in Europe to rivals General Motors Corp and Ford Motor Co with its 1996 sales of a little more than 102,000 vehicles. GM's Opel brand and Ford are big European players with double-digit market shares.
Chrysler, on the other hand, has less than one percent of the European market.
But Adams said Chrysler, which returned to Europe in 1987 after pulling out in the 1970s when the Detroit carmaker faced bankruptcy, has been making excellent progress.
"We are a relatively small player but our business has been growing at more than 20 percent for several years," he said.

Chrysler took another step toward building its brand image in Europe on Tuesday when it announced that it has bought back distribution rights for its cars in Germany, the Netherlands and Belgium from the Louwman Group.
The carmaker has taken similar action in Austria, Brazil, Argentina, France, Italy and Japan during the last 18 months.
"Our goal has always been to grow the Chrysler business in these markets," Adams said of the change in the relationship with the independently-owned dealers in the countries.

Chrysler said the network supporting sales and services of Chrysler and Jeep products in Germany, the Netherlands and Belgium consists of 333 dealers. Combined sales in the three countries for 1996 totalled almost 28,000 units.
Adams said sales remain good for Chrysler's minivan, which makes up more than 40 percent of the carmaker's European sales, and also for the Jeep products, which account for 35 percent.
The remaining balance is made up of Chrysler passenger cars imported from the United States.
To help step up Chrysler's presence in Europe, Adams said the carmaker will offer diesel engines in two to three years.
Chrylser will also offer a new 1.6-litre gasoline engine being developed with BMW AG and built in South America in its Neon model around the turn of the century.
Chrysler vehicles made in the U.S. and sold in Europe include the Neon, Vision and Stratus cars along with the Jeep Cherokee and Wrangler vehicles.
"The cars we sell in Europe have been adapted to suit the expectations of European consumers in terms of vehicle ride and handling dynamics," Adams said.

"We are seeing evidence that there are plenty of Europeans looking for something different, from a design and feel standpoint and also a value standpoint. The American car can offer them something different."
